note: Hand-written definitions of chess terms that are not (yet) concepts with verified examples. Text only: nothing here is checked by an engine, and the app says so wherever it is shown. 'broader' is the concept whose verified examples cover this term; 'related' are concepts worth practising next.

terms.definition: A windmill is a repeated discovered check: one piece moves back and forth, uncovering check from a rook or bishop behind it each time, and uses every move to capture something.

A desperado is a piece that is lost anyway (trapped, or about to be captured) and grabs as much material as it can before it goes — often by capturing with check, so the opponent has no time to take it for free.

The Greek gift is a bishop sacrifice on h7 (or h2) against a castled king, usually followed by a knight check on g5 (g4) and the queen joining the attack. It only works when those follow-up moves really are available, so check the defender's replies before sacrificing.
In an epaulette mate the king is boxed in on both sides by its own pieces (often rooks), like shoulder pads, and a queen gives check from directly in front of it.

The Philidor position is the key drawing method in rook and pawn against rook. The defending king stands in front of the pawn, and the defending rook holds the third rank counted from its own side, keeping the enemy king out. Once the pawn steps onto that rank, the rook goes to the far end of the board and checks the king from behind.
Zugzwang is a position where the side to move would be fine if it could pass, but every legal move makes its position worse. It decides many king and pawn endgames.

Triangulation is a king manoeuvre in the endgame: the king walks around a small triangle of squares to lose one move, so the same position appears with the opponent to move — often putting them in zugzwang.
Perpetual check is a series of checks the opponent can't escape. The same position repeats and the game is drawn — a saving resource when you are behind.

A stalemate trick is a saving idea for the side that is losing: if your king has no safe moves, try to give away or block your remaining pieces so that you are left with no legal move. If it is your turn and you have no legal move but are not in check, the game is a draw.
An x-ray is an attack or defence through an enemy piece: a rook, bishop or queen stands behind that piece on the same line, and as soon as the piece moves or is exchanged, the line opens.
A decoy lures an enemy piece — often the king or queen — onto a square where a tactic then hits it, for example a fork. It usually costs material first, so it is a kind of sacrifice.
Interference means putting a piece between an enemy piece and the square or piece it defends, cutting the line of defence so that something becomes undefended.
An outpost is a square in or near the enemy half that no enemy pawn can attack, ideally protected by one of your own pawns. A knight on an outpost is very hard to drive away.

The pawn structure is the arrangement of both sides' pawns. Pawns can't move backwards, so it changes slowly and decides where the pieces belong and which plans make sense. Its main features are isolated, doubled, backward and passed pawns.

An isolated pawn has no friendly pawns on the files next to it. No pawn can ever protect it, so it can become a target, and the square in front of it is often a strong square for the opponent's pieces.
Doubled pawns are two pawns of the same colour on one file, created by a capture. They can't protect each other and are often — not always — a weakness.

A backward pawn has fallen behind the pawns on the files next to it and can't safely advance, because the square in front of it is controlled by an enemy pawn. It is hard to protect and easy to attack.
An open file has no pawns on it. Rooks belong on open files, where they can reach deep into the enemy position; a half-open file has only enemy pawns on it.
A fianchetto develops a bishop to the long diagonal by moving the knight's pawn one square: g3 and Bg2 (or b3 and Bb2) for White, g6 and Bg7 (or b6 and Bb7) for Black.

Calculation is working out moves in your head before you play them. A simple method: list the forcing moves (checks, captures and threats), look at the opponent's best answer to each, and only then choose.
